question_name: Prior art for this exact anti-tamper class on similar cheap Rockchip devices
findings: No community report was found that names TXCZ, 'com.shzhtxcz', 'rk3326_sgo', or this exact HY300-badged projector as having a documented whole-/system-partition-repopulation-every-cold-boot bug or anti-tamper feature. Targeted searches (English and Chinese: '开机自动还原系统分区', '防root', '分区保护') and Russian (4pda.to) turned up only generic RK3326/RK3229/RK3328 flashing/bricking threads, none matching the specific symptom. XDA has a 'txcz-rk3229-mxq-v2.2' firmware-request thread and a 'TXCZ-20 / SoSoon TP-9058' thread, confirming TXCZ is a real, recognized cheap Chinese STB ODM/board-marking across multiple Rockchip SoCs (RK3229 as well as RK3326), but neither thread discusses persistence/anti-tamper behavior -- both are ordinary 'need firmware for my box' requests. So there is no TXCZ-specific or rk3326_sgo-specific precedent to cite directly. However, three distinct, well-documented prior-art mechanism classes were found that produce the exact symptom shape (silent, unconditional, pre-init /system-equivalent restoration on every cold boot) on other cheap/embedded Android hardware, and one broader industry pattern that names the general product category: (1) HTC T-Mobile G2 / Desire Z 'NAND lock' (2010) -- the single closest historical analog found. HTC devices in 'S-ON' state check a '@secuflag' value in radio NVRAM from the bootloader (HBOOT); when set, HBOOT enforces a NAND/eMMC write-protect lock on the system, boot, and recovery partitions such that 'a reboot loses root, and writes on these partitions won't stick' (technotif.com), i.e. behaviorally indistinguishable from a full restore-to-pristine on every boot. This was defeated purely in software by the 'gfree' exploit (Scott Walker/'Napalm', GPLv3, Dec 2010): a Linux kernel module power-cycled the eMMC chip, cleared the @secuflag, and installed an MMC block-request filter in the kernel to remove write protection on the hidden radio-settings partition -- combining several existing kernel/baseband exploits, requiring no bootloader reflash and no hardware access. This is the strongest precedent for 'defeated via software-only kernel-side fix, no reflash needed.' (2) eMMC-spec 'Power-On Write Protection' (POWP / USER_WP register, eMMC 4.3+) applied at the earliest bootloader stage to 'important partitions' -- documented generically in eMMC vendor specs and, concretely for exactly this STB/smart-terminal use case, in Chinese patent CN105069381A ('Intelligent-terminal-based partition protection method and system'), which claims applying eMMC Power-On Write Protection to designated partitions at the bootloader ('LK' -- Little Kernel, i.e. the MediaTek analog of U-Boot) stage, keyed off boot-mode detection (normal vs recovery), with protection temporarily lifted only for FOTA update flows. This describes the identical mechanism CLASS (hardware write-protect re-armed by the bootloader on every boot, before any OS code runs) on a different but architecturally parallel cheap-STB SoC family (MediaTek, not Rockchip), confirming this is a known, patented, productized Chinese-industry anti-tamper technique for exactly this device category, not a one-off. No Rockchip-specific patent or vendor SDK document describing an equivalent feature was found, but the technique is SoC-agnostic (it lives in eMMC controller registers, not silicon-specific logic) and Rockchip's own U-Boot exposes the same MMC write-protect command primitives. (3) The generic 'reboot to restore' product category (Wikipedia: 'Reboot to restore software... restores that configuration every time the device restarts') is a recognized commercial software class, but virtually all shipping examples found (Faronics Deep Freeze, Horizon DataSys, etc.) are Windows-centric OS-level agents that run post-boot, not pre-init bootloader mechanisms -- not a mechanism-level match, only a naming/category match. Separately and importantly: this device's own prior local research (see project memory hy300_device_findings.md) has already narrowed the leading candidate mechanism to AOSP's own stock 'fs_mgr_overlayfs' adb-remount-for-development feature, NOT a bespoke anti-piracy lock. Official AOSP documentation (android.googlesource.com/.../fs_mgr/README.overlayfs.md) confirms overlayfs write support backs onto either a dynamic 'scratch' partition (A/B devices with free space in super) or '/cache/overlay/' (non-A/B devices) -- and this device's own already-confirmed super/liblp metadata shows NO scratch partition exists in super. If '/cache' itself is reformatted, absent, or backed by tmpfs on this Android-Go non-A/B build (plausible on a stripped-down Go SKU), fs_mgr's overlay upper directory would be recreated empty on every boot by ordinary stock AOSP code -- fully explaining a silent, complete, pre-init-parseable revert of any /system-directory write, with NO malicious anti-piracy intent required at all, and with a well-known, purely-software Google-documented fix path (adb disable-verity + adb remount against a working scratch partition, or fastboot-provisioning a scratch partition into super). This is a materially different, much lower-risk hypothesis than the HTC-style hardware NAND-lock/POWP precedent, and no other Rockchip-STB community report was found where this exact overlayfs-without-scratch failure mode was independently diagnosed and named as such, though it is a logical, previously-documented consequence of stock AOSP overlayfs behavior on any non-A/B device lacking persistent scratch backing, not an invention specific to this device.
relevance_to_our_symptoms: Partial explanation, split across two competing but not mutually exclusive candidate classes, neither of which is confirmed on THIS device by community precedent (no TXCZ/rk3326_sgo report exists either way). The HTC-style NAND-lock/eMMC-POWP class (findings 1-2) would fully explain every observed detail -- restoration into both Recovery and normal Android, before init.rc parses, with a 'fresh inode' appearance for a file that never existed in the pristine build -- because it operates below the filesystem entirely: writes to the protected LBA range either never actually commit to flash (silently accepted by a permissive/buggy MMC driver layer while physically discarded by the eMMC controller) or are explicitly reset by the bootloader's own restore step before the kernel ever mounts the partition, so anything read back is indistinguishable from 'never written.' This class requires no active per-boot 'copy a golden image' step to explain the symptom -- simple write-protection re-armed every power-on is sufficient, matching the emphasis on COLD boot specifically (power-on-write-protect state is tied to power cycling, not warm/soft reboot, in the eMMC spec). The fs_mgr_overlayfs-without-scratch class (finding 3) ALSO fully explains every observed detail via an entirely different, much more mundane route: if the overlay upper directory is torn down and recreated fresh (either because it's tmpfs, or /cache is reformatted at early boot), every write to /system silently vanishes by design, appearing identical to a partition-level restore from userspace's point of view, and this also happens 'before init.rc is parsed' in the sense that first-stage init sets up the overlayfs mount during early fs_mgr processing, prior to second-stage init parsing init.rc. Neither hypothesis is preferred by outside prior art here -- this research item can only report that both mechanism classes are real, documented, and produce indistinguishable symptoms from the outside; distinguishing them requires the device-side static/binary analysis this project's other research items are already pursuing (specifically: whether the 'system' mount point in the live filesystem is itself the raw partition device or an overlayfs mount -- checkable via `mount` output or `/proc/mounts` showing 'overlay' as the fstype -- which the project's own next-session plan already flags as the key discriminating, zero-risk, on-device check).
confidence: medium -- the two candidate mechanism classes (HTC NAND-lock/eMMC-POWP and AOSP fs_mgr_overlayfs) are each independently well-documented with citable primary sources, so confidence in THEIR existence and behavior is high; confidence that either one specifically applies to this TXCZ/rk3326_sgo device is low, since no direct report tying either mechanism to this vendor or SoC family was found -- this is analogy-based prior art, not a confirmed match.
sources_or_method: WebSearch across English, Chinese (Simplified), and Russian queries targeting: (a) TXCZ/txcz branding directly, (b) rk3326_sgo and generic RK3326/RK3128/RK3566/RK3568 symptom-matching phrases, (c) 'Rockchip anti-rollback boot_android partition restore' and variants, (d) the general 'reboot to restore' software category, (e) eMMC power-on write protection as an Android anti-tamper technique, (f) historical HTC G2/Desire Z NAND-lock case once eMMC-WP search results surfaced it as analogous, and (g) AOSP fs_mgr_overlayfs documentation once the project's own prior local findings (read from project memory file hy300_device_findings.md) identified it as the leading internally-ranked hypothesis. WebFetch was used to pull full text from technotif.com (HTC gfree mechanism detail), Google Patents (CN105069381A claims), and android.googlesource.com (official overlayfs README) rather than relying on search-snippet summaries. No device interaction of any kind was performed, consistent with the desktop-only research constraint.
safe_next_step: On the local decompiled/extracted artifacts already saved in this project (boot backups, ramdisk cpio, ATH liblp/super metadata already parsed per hy300_device_findings.md), check the already-pulled `fstab.rk30board` and any first-stage-init fs_mgr flags for `overlayfs`-related mount options (e.g. look for a `scratch` or `overlay` reference, or absence of a `/cache` line entirely) -- this is a pure local file re-read of artifacts already on disk, zero risk. Separately, continue web research narrowly for 'rockchip-linux u-boot mmc write-protect CMD28 CMD30' and 'Rockchip resource.img backup partition FOTA lock' to see if Rockchip's own (rather than MediaTek's) SDK documents an equivalent eMMC-POWP feature by name, which would upgrade the CN105069381A analogy from cross-vendor to same-vendor.
risky_next_step_if_pursued: If local artifact re-analysis and further web research remain inconclusive, the only way to determine which class actually applies would be an on-device, boot-time check: interrupt boot at Recovery (already known reliable per hy300_device_findings.md) and run `cat /proc/mounts` or `mount` to see whether the current 'system' mount shows fstype `overlay` (confirms fs_mgr_overlayfs, software-only, low risk to fix) versus checking raw partition bytes via `dd` before/after a genuine cold-power-cycle reboot to see if the underlying block device itself changes (would point toward an active bootloader-level restore or eMMC-level write rejection, consistent with the HTC-style hardware-anchored class). This on-device check itself is low-risk (read-only `mount`/`dd` commands, no writes to boot-critical partitions), but if the finding then leads toward pursuing a NAND-lock/eMMC-POWP-style fix (e.g. attempting to clear a write-protect register or patch U-Boot), that follow-on step would require either a kernel-module-style in-place software fix analogous to gfree (moderate risk: wrong MMC command sequence to a write-protected region can corrupt metadata) or reflashing U-Boot/trust (high risk, this device's Maskrom is not reliably software-reachable per existing project findings, making recovery from a bad flash dependent on hardware-level access the user has already flagged as the real blocker).
risk_level: The safe_next_step (local file re-read, further web search) is zero risk. The on-device read-only check (`mount`/`proc/mounts`, or before/after `dd` read of raw blocks) is low risk and reversible. Any follow-on write to MMC write-protect registers or U-Boot/trust reflash is high risk -- brick risk with Maskrom-only recovery, consistent with this project's already-documented conclusion that Maskrom is not reliably reachable via software on this specific board.
